name: Account Compromise Response
description: Step-by-step response to a suspected account compromise. Guides through disabling the user, reviewing activity, checking for data access, resetting credentials, and documenting findings.

steps.title: Disable Compromised Account
steps.description: Suspend the suspected compromised user account to prevent further unauthorized access.

steps.title: Review Recent Activity
steps.description: Examine the actor's audit log events from the last 72 hours. Look for unusual actions, unfamiliar IP addresses, or off-hours activity.

steps.title: Check for Data Access
steps.description: Review git clone operations, repository access events, and any data downloads performed by the compromised account.

steps.title: Reset Credentials
steps.description: Force a password reset, revoke all active sessions, and rotate any PATs or SSH keys associated with the account.

steps.title: Document Findings
steps.description: Record the timeline of events, impact assessment, root cause (if known), and remediation steps taken.

name: Leaked Secret Response
description: Response playbook for when a secret (API key, token, credential) is detected in source code or logs.

steps.title: Identify Secret Scope
steps.description: Determine what the leaked secret provides access to — which systems, APIs, or data stores are at risk.

steps.title: Revoke the Secret
steps.description: Immediately revoke or disable the leaked secret through the issuing service's admin interface.

steps.title: Scan for Usage
steps.description: Check access logs of the affected service for any unauthorized use of the leaked secret.

steps.title: Rotate and Replace
steps.description: Generate a new secret and update all legitimate consumers. Use GitHub Actions secrets or a vault service.

steps.title: Document and Prevent
steps.description: Record the incident. Enable push protection and secret scanning to prevent future leaks.

name: Privilege Escalation Response
description: Response playbook for unauthorized privilege escalation events such as admin role grants or team maintainer self-promotion.

steps.title: Verify Authorization
steps.description: Contact the actor and their manager to determine if the privilege change was authorized through proper channels.

steps.title: Review the Change
steps.description: Examine the specific permission change — what role was granted, to which org/team, and what access it provides.

steps.title: Revert if Unauthorized
steps.description: If the change was not authorized, immediately revert the privilege change through the organization's People settings.

steps.title: Document
steps.description: Record whether the change was authorized or unauthorized, actions taken, and any policy gaps identified.

name: CI/CD Threat Response
description: Response playbook for threats involving GitHub Actions workflows, such as workflow modifications, suspicious runner activity, or secret exfiltration attempts.

steps.title: Disable Affected Workflow
steps.description: Disable the suspicious workflow to prevent further execution. Navigate to the repository's Actions tab.

steps.title: Review Workflow Changes
steps.description: Examine the git history of the workflow file to identify what was changed and by whom. Check for obfuscated code or unusual steps.

steps.title: Check for Data Exfiltration
steps.description: Review workflow run logs for signs of data exfiltration — outbound network calls, artifact uploads, or secret exposure.

steps.title: Remediate
steps.description: Revert the malicious workflow changes, rotate any secrets that may have been exposed, and re-enable with fixes applied.

steps.title: Document
steps.description: Record the attack vector, impact, remediation steps, and any improvements to CI/CD security controls.

name: Runaway Workflow Queue Response
description: Response playbook for runaway GitHub Actions workflow queue alerts. Guides through identifying the source, stopping the runaway automation, and preventing recurrence. GitHub enterprises have a 50,000 pending workflow run queue limit.

steps.title: Identify the Runaway Source
steps.description: Check the detection details for the actor (user or GitHub App) and repository triggering excessive workflow runs. Use the enterprise audit log filtered by 'workflows.created_workflow_run' to identify the specific workflow file and trigger event.

steps.title: Check Current Queue Depth
steps.description: Query the enterprise audit log for pending workflow runs to assess how close to the 50,000 limit the queue is. Use: GET /enterprises/{enterprise}/actions/runs?status=queued

steps.title: Disable the Offending Workflow
steps.description: Navigate to the repository's Actions tab and disable the runaway workflow immediately. If triggered by a GitHub App, suspend the app installation.

steps.title: Cancel Queued Runs
steps.description: Cancel all pending/queued workflow runs from the offending workflow to free queue capacity. Use the Actions API: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/cancel for each queued run, or use the bulk cancel UI.

steps.title: Investigate Root Cause
steps.description: Determine why the automation ran away: recursive workflow triggers (workflow_run events triggering more workflows), misconfigured cron schedules, infinite retry loops, or a compromised GitHub App. Check the workflow YAML for 'workflow_run' triggers that could create cycles.

steps.title: Apply Preventive Controls
steps.description: Add concurrency controls to the workflow (concurrency group with cancel-in-progress), set appropriate rate limits on GitHub App installations, and consider adding a workflow_run filter to prevent recursive triggers.

steps.title: Document and Monitor
steps.description: Record the incident timeline, queue depth reached, root cause, and remediation applied. Monitor the workflow queue depth for 24 hours to confirm the issue is resolved.

name: Defense Evasion Response
description: Response playbook for defense evasion detections such as audit log tampering, IP allowlist changes, SSO bypass attempts, or webhook deletions that may blind security monitoring.

steps.title: Assess Monitoring Impact
steps.description: Determine which security monitoring capabilities were affected. Identify any gaps in visibility created by the change (e.g., webhook deletion removes SIEM feed, IP allowlist change opens network access).

steps.title: Verify Actor Authorization
steps.description: Confirm whether the actor had legitimate business justification for the change. Check change management tickets or approvals.

steps.title: Revert Unauthorized Changes
steps.description: If the change was unauthorized, immediately restore the previous configuration. Re-enable webhooks, restore IP allowlist entries, or re-enforce SSO requirements.

steps.title: Check for Concurrent Attacks
steps.description: Defense evasion often precedes other attacks. Review audit logs for suspicious activity that occurred while monitoring was degraded — look for data exfiltration, privilege escalation, or lateral movement.

steps.title: Strengthen Controls
steps.description: Implement additional safeguards to prevent recurrence: restrict who can modify security settings, enable alerts on configuration changes, and ensure redundant monitoring paths.

steps.title: Escalate if Malicious
steps.description: If the defense evasion appears intentional and coordinated with other suspicious activity, escalate to the security incident response team immediately.

name: Access Control Violation Response
description: Response playbook for access control detections including overly permissive PATs, GitHub App installations with broad access, and external collaborator grants.

steps.title: Identify the Access Scope
steps.description: Determine the exact scope of access granted — which repositories, permissions, and data are now accessible. For PATs, review the scopes. For GitHub Apps, check installation permissions. For collaborators, review repository access.

steps.title: Validate Business Need
steps.description: Contact the actor to understand the business justification. Verify whether the broad access is genuinely needed or if a more restrictive scope would suffice.

steps.title: Apply Least Privilege
steps.description: If the access is overly broad, work with the actor to reduce scope. Replace classic PATs with fine-grained tokens scoped to specific repos. Limit GitHub App installations to selected repositories only.

steps.title: Revoke if Unjustified
steps.description: If no valid business need exists, revoke the token or remove the collaborator access immediately. Notify the actor of the policy requirement.

steps.title: Document and Update Policy
steps.description: Record the access control finding. Update access management policies if gaps are identified. Consider implementing automated guardrails for token creation.

name: Policy Violation Response
description: Response playbook for policy violation detections including push protection bypasses, branch protection overrides, and repeated bypass offenses.

steps.title: Review the Bypass Justification
steps.description: Examine the reason provided for the bypass (if any). Check if the actor followed the exception process or bypassed without authorization.

steps.title: Assess Risk of the Bypass
steps.description: Determine what protection was bypassed and what risk it introduced. For push protection bypasses, verify the secret is not actually sensitive. For branch protection overrides, review what was merged without required checks.

steps.title: Remediate Exposure
steps.description: If the bypass exposed a real secret, follow the Leaked Secret Response playbook. If branch protection was bypassed, review the merged code for security issues.

steps.title: Address Repeat Offenders
steps.description: If this is a repeat offense, escalate to the actor's manager. Consider restricting bypass permissions or requiring additional approval for future exceptions.

steps.title: Document and Reinforce
steps.description: Record the violation, outcome, and any corrective actions. Reinforce the policy with the team and consider security awareness training if patterns emerge.

name: Workflow File Modification Response
description: Response playbook for detecting modifications to GitHub Actions workflow files (.github/workflows/). Workflow changes can introduce malicious CI/CD steps, exfiltrate secrets, or compromise the software supply chain.

steps.title: Identify the Change
steps.description: Review the git diff for the workflow file modification. Identify which repository, branch, and workflow file was changed. Note the actor and timestamp.

steps.title: Analyze Workflow Content
steps.description: Examine the modified workflow for suspicious patterns: new external actions from unverified sources, outbound network calls (curl/wget to unknown hosts), environment variable exfiltration, or obfuscated shell commands.

steps.title: Verify Actor Authorization
steps.description: Confirm the actor is authorized to modify CI/CD workflows. Check if CODEOWNERS requires specific reviewers for .github/workflows/ changes and whether that review occurred.

steps.title: Check Action Pinning
steps.description: Verify that any newly added GitHub Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs rather than mutable tags. Unpinned actions are vulnerable to tag-rewriting supply chain attacks.

steps.title: Review Recent Workflow Runs
steps.description: Check if the modified workflow has already executed. Review run logs for unexpected behavior, failed status checks, or anomalous timing.

steps.title: Revert if Malicious
steps.description: If the workflow change is confirmed malicious, revert the commit immediately. Disable the workflow, rotate any secrets accessible to it, and investigate the actor's other recent activity.

steps.title: Escalate if Supply Chain Attack
steps.description: If the modification appears to be part of a coordinated supply chain attack (e.g., targeting multiple repositories or involving compromised Actions), escalate to the incident response team and notify downstream consumers.

name: Suspicious Runner Registration Response
description: Response playbook for detecting unauthorized self-hosted runner registrations. Rogue runners can execute arbitrary code with access to repository secrets and internal networks.

steps.title: Identify the Runner
steps.description: Determine which runner was registered or brought online. Note the runner name, labels, operating system, and the organization or repository it was registered to.

steps.title: Verify Registration Authorization
steps.description: Check whether the runner registration was requested through approved channels. Verify the registration token was created by an authorized administrator.

steps.title: Check Runner Infrastructure
steps.description: Determine where the runner is hosted. Verify it matches your organization's approved runner infrastructure (e.g., corporate cloud accounts, hardened VMs). Investigate if it's running on unknown or personal infrastructure.

steps.title: Review Runner Activity
steps.description: Check what jobs the runner has executed since registration. Look for workflows that access secrets, deploy to production, or have elevated permissions.

steps.title: Remove Unauthorized Runners
steps.description: If the runner is unauthorized, immediately remove it from the organization. Revoke the registration token and rotate any secrets that may have been exposed to it.

steps.title: Restrict Runner Registration
steps.description: Review and tighten runner registration policies. Consider limiting who can create registration tokens and enabling runner groups to restrict which repositories can use self-hosted runners.

name: Actions Secret Access Spike Response
description: Response playbook for detecting unusual spikes in GitHub Actions secret access. A spike may indicate secret harvesting, compromised workflows, or unauthorized automation accessing credentials.

steps.title: Identify the Source
steps.description: Determine which workflows and repositories are responsible for the spike in secret access. Identify the actor who triggered the workflow runs and the specific secrets being accessed.

steps.title: Compare to Baseline
steps.description: Review historical secret access patterns for the actor and repository. Determine if the spike correlates with legitimate activity (e.g., batch deployments, CI pipeline changes) or is anomalous.

steps.title: Review Workflow Logs
steps.description: Examine the workflow run logs for signs of secret exfiltration — look for base64 encoding of environment variables, outbound HTTP requests to unusual endpoints, or artifact uploads containing sensitive data.

steps.title: Check for Workflow Modifications
steps.description: Verify whether the workflows accessing secrets were recently modified. A workflow change combined with a secret access spike is a strong indicator of compromise.

steps.title: Rotate Exposed Secrets
steps.description: If secret harvesting is confirmed or suspected, immediately rotate all secrets that were accessed during the spike. Update secret values in GitHub Actions and notify dependent services.

steps.title: Restrict Secret Access
steps.description: Review which workflows and environments can access organization secrets. Consider scoping secrets to specific repositories or environments and enabling required approvals for environment deployments.

name: GHAS Feature Disabled Response
description: Response playbook for detecting when GitHub Advanced Security features (secret scanning, code scanning, Dependabot) are disabled. Disabling these features creates blind spots in vulnerability detection.

steps.title: Identify What Was Disabled
steps.description: Determine which GHAS feature was disabled, on which repository or organization, and by whom. Note whether it was secret scanning, code scanning, push protection, or Dependabot alerts.

steps.title: Verify Authorization
steps.description: Contact the actor to confirm the change was intentional and authorized. Check if there is a valid business reason (e.g., repository being archived, license changes, false positive overload).

steps.title: Assess Security Impact
steps.description: Evaluate what vulnerability detection is now missing. For secret scanning, new secrets pushed to the repo will go undetected. For code scanning, new vulnerabilities in PRs will not be flagged. For Dependabot, known CVEs in dependencies will not trigger alerts.

steps.title: Re-enable if Unauthorized
steps.description: If the change was not authorized, immediately re-enable the GHAS feature. Navigate to the repository or organization security settings.

steps.title: Check for Concurrent Suspicious Activity
steps.description: Defense evasion by disabling security tools often precedes an attack. Look for secrets being pushed, vulnerable dependencies being added, or malicious code being introduced while scanning was disabled.

steps.title: Enforce GHAS Policies
steps.description: Consider enabling organization-level enforcement of GHAS features so they cannot be disabled at the repository level. Use organization security policies to require these features on all repositories.

name: Data Exfiltration Response
description: Response playbook for data exfiltration detections including mass repository cloning, repository visibility changes to public, forks to external orgs, and cross-org data access patterns.

steps.title: Quantify Data Exposure
steps.description: Determine the scope of potential data loss. Identify which repositories were accessed, their sensitivity classification, and the volume of data potentially exfiltrated (clone operations, downloads, API access).

steps.title: Identify the Actor
steps.description: Determine whether the actor is an insider (employee, contractor) or external (compromised account, former employee). Check the actor's role, recent access patterns, and employment status.

steps.title: Contain the Breach
steps.description: Immediately restrict the actor's access. Suspend the account if compromise is suspected. If a repository was made public, revert visibility immediately. Revoke any tokens or SSH keys associated with the actor.

steps.title: Assess Sensitive Data Impact
steps.description: Review the accessed repositories for sensitive content: API keys, credentials, PII, proprietary algorithms, or compliance-regulated data. Determine if any regulatory notification requirements are triggered.

steps.title: Preserve Evidence
steps.description: Capture audit logs, access records, and any available network logs. Document the timeline of access events for potential legal or HR proceedings.

steps.title: Escalate to Legal/HR
steps.description: If intentional data theft is confirmed, escalate to legal counsel and HR. Determine if law enforcement notification is required based on data classification and regulatory requirements.

name: Branch Protection Tampering Response
description: Response playbook for detections involving branch protection rule deletion, modification, or ruleset changes that weaken code review and merge safeguards.

steps.title: Identify the Change
steps.description: Determine which repository's branch protection was modified or deleted, which branch was affected (typically main/master), and what specific protections were weakened or removed.

steps.title: Verify Authorization
steps.description: Confirm the change was made through an approved change management process. Check if the actor had a legitimate reason (e.g., emergency hotfix, migration) and whether it was approved by a repository admin or security team.

steps.title: Check for Unauthorized Merges
steps.description: Review the branch's git history for any commits merged while protections were disabled. Look for unreviewed code, force pushes, or merges that bypassed required status checks.

steps.title: Restore Protections
steps.description: Immediately restore branch protection rules to their previous state. Re-enable required reviews, status checks, and other safeguards.

steps.title: Audit Merged Code
steps.description: If code was merged while protections were down, conduct a thorough review of those changes. Check for backdoors, malicious dependencies, or security vulnerabilities introduced without proper review.

steps.title: Restrict Branch Protection Admin
steps.description: Review who has permission to modify branch protection rules. Consider using organization-level rulesets that cannot be overridden by repository admins.

name: Impossible Travel and Anomalous Login Response
description: Response playbook for impossible travel detections, Tor exit node logins, brute force attempts, and dormant account reactivations that indicate potential credential compromise.

steps.title: Verify with the User
steps.description: Contact the account owner through a known-good channel (not email, which may be compromised). Ask if they are traveling, using a VPN, or recognize the login activity.

steps.title: Check Login Context
steps.description: Review the login event details: IP addresses, geolocation, user agent, authentication method (password vs. SSO vs. token). Determine if the login used MFA or bypassed it.

steps.title: Suspend if Unverified
steps.description: If the user cannot be reached or does not recognize the activity, immediately suspend the account and revoke all active sessions.

steps.title: Review Post-Login Activity
steps.description: Examine what actions were performed after the suspicious login. Look for repository access, settings changes, token creation, or data downloads that may indicate the account was used maliciously.

steps.title: Force Credential Reset
steps.description: Require the user to reset their password, re-enroll MFA, and rotate any PATs or SSH keys. Verify that recovery email and phone number have not been changed.

steps.title: Block Suspicious IPs
steps.description: If the login came from a known malicious IP or Tor exit node, consider adding it to the organization's IP deny list or blocking at the network level.

name: Supply Chain Dependency Attack Response
description: Response playbook for supply chain attacks involving dependency confusion, typosquatting, malicious packages, compromised maintainers, and unusual package sources.

steps.title: Identify the Malicious Package
steps.description: Determine which package triggered the alert: its name, version, registry source, and which repository's lockfile or manifest references it. Check if it is a typosquat, dependency confusion, or known-malicious package.

steps.title: Check if Package Was Installed
steps.description: Determine if the malicious package was actually installed in CI or on developer machines. Review workflow run logs, build artifacts, and developer environments for evidence of execution.

steps.title: Remove the Package
steps.description: Immediately remove the malicious package from the manifest/lockfile. Pin legitimate dependencies to known-good versions. Create a PR to revert the dependency change.

steps.title: Assess Compromise Scope
steps.description: If the package executed, determine what it had access to. Check for credential theft (env vars, .npmrc, .pypirc), data exfiltration (outbound network), or persistence mechanisms (modified scripts, cron jobs).

steps.title: Rotate Exposed Credentials
steps.description: Rotate any credentials that were accessible during package execution: CI secrets, registry tokens, cloud provider keys, and developer machine credentials.

steps.title: Implement Preventive Controls
steps.description: Configure package registry scoping (e.g., npm scope to private registry), enable lockfile-only installs in CI, set up Dependabot or Socket.dev for dependency monitoring, and require review for lockfile changes.

name: Cross-Organization Threat Response
description: Response playbook for detections that span multiple organizations within an enterprise, including cross-org admin escalation, cross-org secret alerts, and rapid cross-org repository access.

steps.title: Map the Cross-Org Activity
steps.description: Identify all organizations involved in the alert. Determine the timeline of activity across each organization and the actor performing the actions.

steps.title: Verify Enterprise Context
steps.description: Confirm whether the actor legitimately operates across multiple organizations (e.g., platform team, enterprise admin). Check their enterprise role and responsibilities.

steps.title: Assess Coordination
steps.description: Determine if the cross-org activity appears coordinated or automated. Check for patterns suggesting a compromised account being used to escalate access broadly across the enterprise.

steps.title: Contain Across All Orgs
steps.description: If the activity is unauthorized, suspend the actor's access across ALL affected organizations simultaneously. Coordinate with org admins to prevent the actor from pivoting to other orgs.

steps.title: Review Enterprise Audit Log
steps.description: Use the enterprise audit log to get a complete picture of the actor's activity across all organizations. Look for additional suspicious actions not yet detected.

steps.title: Escalate to Enterprise Security
steps.description: Cross-org threats indicate a potentially enterprise-wide compromise. Notify the enterprise security team, consider engaging incident response, and evaluate if credential reset is needed at the enterprise level.
